title: A sorted query that slows each month
question: The "recent orders" page runs WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. There is an index on customer_id, yet the query gets slower every month for the biggest customers. What fixes it?
context: PostgreSQL, 80 million orders. The largest customers have hundreds of thousands of rows each. EXPLAIN shows an index scan on customer_id followed by a sort.

options.label: Add a second index, on created_at, so the ORDER BY can use it too
options.why: Two single-column indexes do not combine into an ordered walk. The planner can use one to find the customer's rows or the other to walk by date, but not both — so it still fetches every matching row, or walks the whole table by date looking for this customer.

options.label: Replace it with a composite index on (customer_id, created_at)
options.why: The index then stores each customer's rows already in date order, so the database jumps to the customer and reads the first twenty entries — no sort, and the cost stays the same whether the customer has a hundred orders or a million.

options.label: Cache each customer's recent orders in Redis for a minute
options.why: It hides the cost for repeat visits and makes a new order invisible for up to a minute. The first request for each customer still pays for the full fetch and sort, and that is the request getting slower.

options.label: Partition the orders table by month to keep each part small
options.why: Partitioning by time helps queries that filter by time. This one filters by customer and sorts by time across all months, so it now touches every partition — often slower than before.
